title: Fracture
full_review:
"Fracture" (New Line) is a generally effective mystery thriller about a wealthy aeronautical engineer, Ted Crawford (Anthony Hopkins), who shoots his unfaithful wife, Jennifer (Embeth Davidtz).

The detective and hostage negotiator, Rob Nunally (Billy Burke), who comes to the house to reason with Crawford, gets the surprise of his life when he looks closely at the unconscious victim on the floor. It's his lover, whom he had previously known only as "Mrs. Smith."

How Crawford could have known that it would be Nunally who would be assigned to the case, as he clearly did (for this was part of his revenge strategy) is one of many fanciful plot elements.

The distraught Nunally wants Crawford prosecuted at all costs, given his personal interest, and is not above rigging evidence to make sure nothing goes wrong.

Meanwhile, the incarcerated Crawford handpicks (huh?) career-minded young assistant district attorney Willy Beachum (Ryan Gosling), knowing that Beachum has already tendered his resignation to boss district attorney Joe Lobruto (David Straitharn), has a lucrative job waiting for him with a corporate law firm, and will probably give this case short shrift. For his own part, Crawford eschews legal counsel, and says he'll defend himself.

Crawford -- who can find structural flaws in planes and such -- tells Beachum he can see the crack in anything or anyone, referring to Beachum's ambition (not to mention the legal technicality that will lead to his acquittal).

Beachum is indeed anxious to put this case behind him and get on to the new job, where he has already commenced an affair with his new boss, high-powered attorney Nikki Gardner (Rosamund Pike), who pressures him to dump the Crawford case, and start his new assignment -- and life with her -- posthaste.

Beachum has a big problem, though. He can't nail Crawford unless the gun used to shoot his wife is found. And repeated thorough searches of the house turn up nothing.

Director Gregory Hoblit's detached style and the stylishly cold production design, both intentional, prove a bit distancing, and, of course, we know who the killer is. But the suspense derives from seeing if the cocky Crawford will indeed get away with it.

The antagonists are compelling. Gosling conveys much interesting shading in his portrayal, and Hopkins uses his innate intelligence and tauntingly humorous mien to good effect. The cat-and-mouse interplay between these two is reminiscent of the Michael Caine-Laurence Olivier face-off in "Sleuth."

Daniel Pyne and Glenn Gers' mostly literate script tries hard to avoid the predictable, though plot holes abound.

Several ethical issues such as whether Beachum will see the Crawford case to a satisfactory conclusion, and his actions involving Crawford's comatose wife, add further texture to the whole. In each instance, they are satisfactorily resolved.

The film contains brief shots of the shooting, suicide, murder, rough language and vulgar expressions and profanity, innuendo, adultery and implied premarital encounters. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
